2.add: An isolated eye pair that supports an action is sufficient for that action under the test conditions, which gives the anterior lateral eyes a real role in predation alongside the principal eyes.

3.add: The dot removes the changing shape and irregular movement of a live fly, so the orientation reflects detection of a small moving target by the anterior lateral eyes.

4.add: Contrast sets the strength of the visual signal, angular diameter sets how much of the retina the target occupies, and speed sets how quickly the signal crosses successive receptors, so a stimulus effective at one contrast can become much less effective at another at the same speed.

5.add: The same sensory stimulus can have a different behavioral consequence depending on feeding state, so an absent turn in a recently fed spider can reflect a decision not to pursue instead of an invisible target.

6.add: A long focal length enlarges the image at the retina, which gives fine angular sampling, and the accompanying restricted field makes accurate alignment with a target necessary.

7.add: Light can pass through the more anterior receptor regions before reaching deeper ones, and the central restriction of the upper layers means that different parts of the retina do not contain an identical stack of receptors.

third_paragraph.8: Fine sampling permits small spatial differences to reach separate receptor positions. A microscopic receptor separation becomes an angular sampling interval through the optical magnification of the lens, which is how Land related the receptor mosaic to the image that the lens produces. The colored section locates the corresponding layered organ in Hasarius.

9.add: A change in object distance moves the sharp image plane relative to the receptor layers even when the lens does not change shape, so objects at different distances are sharply imaged on different layers. Land's early proposal that particular layers carry receptors tuned to particular colors was later tested by physiological and molecular measurements of receptor sensitivity and pigment localization.

10.add: These landmarks provide anatomical references for a comparable pathway, in which the layered retinal inputs retain some anatomical separation as they enter successive processing regions.

11.add: Under red and green light, the same target at the same physical distance generates a different pattern of focus across the retinal layers, and Nagata's account links that difference to a predicted error in perceived distance.

12.add: A graded depolarization encodes stimulus strength through its amplitude, and the 5-mV calibration and 100 ms flash duration express the response in millivolts and the stimulus in time. The colored Hasarius section shows the layered organ of the principal eye to which this physiology relates.

13.add: The sensitivity measurement compares the light required to evoke a specified electrical response, which separates wavelength preference from differences in the brightness of the flashes. Later pigment localization in Hasarius places an ultraviolet-sensitive pigment in the upper retinal layers.

14.add: The green class differs from the ultraviolet class in the wavelength that requires the least light for a response, a physiological distinction taken from voltage recordings in individual cells, whereas the purified pigment's absorption spectrum identifies a molecular property.

15.add: A dual-peaked sensitivity curve means that two separated wavelength regions can effectively activate one recorded cell, and the within-cell comparison shows that ultraviolet and green flashes evoke responses with different time courses in the same receptor.

16.add: The green-sensitive pigment spans the two deeper layers and the ultraviolet-sensitive pigment occupies the upper layers, so a simple assignment of one color to one depth does not hold: a green-sensitive receptor can receive a blurred green image, and optical sharpness can carry information independently of the pigment's wavelength preference.

17.add: Jump distance remained closely related to prey distance, and the hunting observations found no movement before the jump that would generate useful motion parallax, which narrows the plausible cues to monocular ones such as image focus.

18.add: Red illumination changes optical focus as well as pigment stimulation, and the shortening of the jump agrees with the direction predicted if the spider interprets increased blur using a relationship appropriate to green light. Green-sensitive Rh1 can still absorb red light, less efficiently, because a pigment's sensitivity extends beyond its peak.

19.add: Raising the red intensity sixfold left the direction and approximate magnitude of the error intact, so a reduction in effective brightness is inadequate to explain the wavelength effect.

20.add: Blur depends on both object distance and the position of the receptor layer relative to focus, so a fixed optical system converts distance into a measurable property of the retinal image. The anatomical layers, wavelength manipulation and jump measurements support the cue.

21.add: The predicted red curve combines the measured pigment properties with the filter's measured spectral transmission and peaks near 626 nm, so an additional effective spectral channel arises from filtering an existing pigment class instead of from an additional opsin.

23.add: A third effective receptor sensitivity can be produced by filtering an existing pigment class, so trichromatic potential does not require three different opsin proteins. Absorbing short wavelengths improves spectral separation but leaves fewer photons available to the filtered receptors, a cost under dim illumination that follows from the optical properties.

24.add: Muscles acting on the retinal tube move the sampled image without a conspicuous rotation of the external eye, with four displacing muscles producing horizontal or vertical shifts of the sampled direction and the two wrapping bands rotating the retina and changing the orientation of its receptor rows relative to a target.

third_paragraph.25: Six axons could be traced to the six muscles, which identifies the final motor supply to the movable retinal tube. Sensory axons carry information inward from the retina, whereas motor axons deliver commands to the muscles that move it, and Land distinguished these routes anatomically instead of treating every fiber beside the eye as sensory.

27.add: Target displacement produced an abrupt directed movement toward the target followed by a slower return, whereas spontaneous records were more variable and could continue without any stimulation, so the two movement classes have distinguishable motor traces and different dependence on visual input.

28.add: Land elicited directed shifts through stimulation visible to different eye pairs, which indicates that principal-eye motor control is not restricted to information first detected by the principal retina, and retinal tracking is a motor output distinct from body orientation.

29.add: The horizontal cycles recur more rapidly than the large torsional excursion, so a target can be swept repeatedly at one orientation before the receptor rows reach a substantially different orientation, which supports an active sampling strategy.

31.add: The first response began after the entire dot entered the visible field, which indicates that entry of the target into the lateral field matters, and the response rate varied with target position.

32.add: Larger eccentricities produced larger movements that were also faster, which reduces how much longer a large turn takes, and repeated saccades reduce the remaining error.

33.add: In a freely turning spider the target shifts across the retina as the body rotates toward it, which can signal when to correct or stop the movement, and separate stimulus and ring traces made the attempted turn measurable without that consequence.

34.add: A complete turn is defined by its relation to the target direction, so the expected movement varies with target angle, and many recorded turns closely matched that angle while smaller partial turns formed a separate class that often left a substantial target error.

35.add: The spider received the target information before darkness and completed its attempted turn afterward, so accurate complete responses indicate a command that can persist after the visual stimulus is no longer available. Complete and partial movements remained behaviorally distinct, and habituation could alter which response was selected.

36.add: Eye tracking recorded the position and orientation of the principal retinas in the restrained spider, so changing lateral-eye availability tested a sensory contribution to this internal motor output, and the use of several target sizes and speeds reduced dependence on one moving-dot condition. The measured output is internal retinal motion, distinct from the body saccades in the Servaea ball assays.

37.add: A stationary target can be examined by moving the principal retina across it without lateral-eye guidance, so scanning and tracking have different sensory dependencies, and cricket and oval stimuli recruited different degrees of examination.

third_paragraph.38: Retinal separation and position describe where the sampled regions move, whereas retinal angle describes torsion, and two retinas can change their relative distance without rotating by the same amount. Stationary cricket stimuli elicited more examination and torsional movement than oval stimuli when lateral vision was available, a measured stimulus-dependent difference in motor pattern. The published position axis uses the eye tracker's pixel coordinates, whereas the presented targets are specified in degrees.

39.add: Synapsin labeling marks regions rich in presynaptic machinery and tubulin labeling makes processes and tracts easier to trace, and the two together reveal a clear connection from AM1 to AM2 and another toward the arcuate body.

40.add: A shared second-order neuropil can receive information that arrived through two different first-order regions, and the posterior median route differs from the lateral routes, so the secondary eyes are not all assigned to one identical circuit.

41.add: Waveform-based sorting distinguishes candidate units for analysis of individual response patterns, and the recording region in or near the arcuate body relates the physiology to central visual anatomy.

42.add: Position, velocity and direction describe different properties of the target, and a unit can depend on more than one of them, so the results indicate complex visual selectivity in central units for particular parts of the target's trajectory.

43.add: An intact and a scrambled stimulus share many local image elements while differing in arrangement, so the comparison addresses configuration sensitivity more directly than a comparison with a blank field, and the response of the example unit also depended on position.

44.add: Removing one eye system changed whether a structured field could be recovered, so a unit that required both inputs is not explained by an independent response from either system alone, and the interval of roughly 80–160 ms before the spikes constrains the timing of the response-related pattern. The anatomical pathways mapped in Marpissa supply a comparative account of how such inputs can converge.

third_paragraph.45: The candidate transmitter is localized in the processes that carry sensory information into the brain, and its presence in the terminal regions is consistent with a chemical role in transmission from photoreceptors, a histaminergic pathway. Antibody labeling reports molecular recognition in tissue, whereas release, receptor activation and membrane current during a visual stimulus require physiological measurement.

inserts.title: Angular size describes a target from the spider's viewpoint
paragraphs: Angular size is the extent of an object at the eye, measured in degrees, and it is independent of the object's physical size. A single angular diameter can be produced by different physical objects at different distances, so degrees describe the stimulus as the receptor array experiences it.

Zurek and colleagues placed screens 150 mm from the spider and varied the angular diameter of dark dots against a gray background. A 4° dot is the same visual stimulus whether a small target is near or a larger one is farther away, because the dot is specified at the eye.

The dots ranged from 0.5° to 8° in diameter, so the stimulus set spanned targets that occupy very different fractions of the retina. Angular size is the relevant variable for comparing a stimulus with the receptor array.
notes: Angular size is the quantity that links a stimulus to the receptor array, because it describes the target from the spider's viewpoint.
Degrees at the eye.
A four-degree dot can be produced by objects of different physical size at different distances, so angular size is the appropriate variable for comparing stimuli.
The two display screens stood 150 mm from the spider and were separated by 120°.
Controlled targets.
A controlled dot removes the changing shape and irregular movement of a live fly.
A blank screen provides the comparison for turns that occur without a visible moving target.
Why a ball is used.
The spider's feet rotate a lightweight polystyrene ball, so an attempted turn is recorded while stimulus position remains under experimental control.
The display covers known directions relative to the anterior lateral eyes, which allows detection to be tied to a defined part of the visual field.
The measured response.
The recorded variable is the frequency of orientation, which reflects detection of the moving target and the decision to turn.

inserts.title: A movable retina steers the sampled direction
paragraphs: In the principal eye of Phidippus and Metaphidippus, the lens is fixed in the carapace while the long retinal tube behind it can move. Moving the tube changes which direction is sampled through the lens, so the small receptor array can be aimed at different parts of the scene without turning the eye.

The long focal length of the principal eye enlarges the image at the retina. Enlargement gives fine angular sampling, and the accompanying restricted field makes accurate alignment between the retina and a target necessary.

The anterior lateral eyes provide the contrasting arrangement, a broad viewing field without a movable tube. A broad lateral field and a restricted principal field give different spatial access to a target, with the lateral eyes covering a wide region and the principal retina sampling a small part of it at high resolution.
notes: The principal eye separates the position of the external lens from the position of the retina, which allows aiming to happen inside the eye.
Lens and retina move independently.
The lens is fixed in the carapace, but the long retinal assembly can move, changing the direction sampled through the lens.
The external eye needs no conspicuous rotation for the sampled image to change.
Magnification and a restricted field.
A long focal length enlarges the image at the retina, which supports fine angular sampling.
The restricted field makes accurate alignment with a target necessary, so the retina must be positioned on the object of interest.
Two eye systems with different fields.
Land compared the optical organization of the principal eyes with the broader viewing arrangement of the anterior lateral eyes.
The anterior lateral eyes cover a broad field, whereas the principal eyes sample a restricted region at higher resolution.
Why both systems matter.
Lateral vision supports detection and orientation toward a target, while the principal retina samples the target in detail once it is aligned.
The two systems contribute different operations to predation.

inserts.title: Object distance moves the sharp image across layers
paragraphs: Focus is the optical condition in which rays from an object form a comparatively sharp image at a receptor plane. The principal retina has receptor layers at different depths behind a fixed optical system, so the sharp image of a near object and the sharp image of a far object fall on different layers.

For blue-green light, Land found the best image near L2, while the deeper L1 could receive a focused image from an object at approximately 2 cm under the reported optical conditions. These values belong to a specific combination of wavelength, layer and optical conditions.

Because the layers sit at different image distances, retinal depth is relevant to viewing distance: the same object can be sharp on one layer and blurred on another. The layered geometry can be retained while the assignment of a color to each layer is revised by later measurements.
notes: In a layered retina behind a fixed lens, the distance of an object determines which layer receives the sharpest image.
Image plane and receptor layers.
A change in object distance moves the sharp image plane relative to the receptor layers even when the lens does not change shape.
An object therefore need not be equally sharp in every layer.
What Land measured.
Land related the sectioned retina to optical observations of the image.
For blue-green light the best image approached L2, and an object at approximately 2 cm could form a focused image on the deeper L1 under the reported conditions.
Optics and pigments are separate questions.
An optical prediction describes where images are sharp, and a pigment measurement describes which wavelengths a receptor absorbs.
Later work retained the layered geometry while revising the early proposal that a specific layer holds receptors tuned to one color.
Why distance matters to the eye.
Retinal depth makes the layered organ relevant to viewing distance, which the jump-distance experiments in Hasarius test with wavelength manipulations.

inserts.title: Graded potentials encode stimulus strength by amplitude
paragraphs: A graded potential is a change in membrane voltage whose size depends on the strength of the stimulus. DeVoe's recordings from principal-eye photoreceptors in Phidippus regius showed graded depolarizations: the membrane voltage became less negative by an amount that depended on the flash.

Depolarization names the direction of the voltage change and does not by itself mean that the cell fires action potentials. An action potential has a fixed size, whereas a receptor's graded response carries information in its amplitude.

DeVoe used calibrated flashes lasting 100 ms and a 5-mV voltage reference, so each response is expressed in millivolts and each stimulus in time. Varying wavelength and intensity while measuring response amplitude made it possible to compare the sensitivity of individual receptors to different wavelengths.
notes: A light-sensitive receptor can encode stimulus strength through the amplitude of a graded voltage change.
Graded versus all-or-none.
A graded potential varies continuously with stimulus strength.
An action potential is a brief event of fixed size that signals by its timing.
What depolarization means.
Depolarization makes the membrane potential less negative, which names the direction of the change.
It does not establish by itself that the cell generates action potentials.
Calibrated measurements.
The 5-mV calibration expresses the recording in millivolts, while the 100 ms flash duration expresses the time over which the receptor was stimulated.
Comparing responses to calibrated flashes of different wavelengths in individual cells allows sensitivity to be compared across wavelengths.
The preparation.
Intracellular recording places an electrode inside the cell, so the voltage change in the receptor itself is measured.
DeVoe recorded principal-eye photoreceptors in Phidippus regius.
From voltage to sensitivity.
Because response amplitude depends on stimulus strength, the light needed to evoke a chosen amplitude measures a receptor's sensitivity at each wavelength.
Plotting that sensitivity against wavelength gives the spectral sensitivity curves of the ultraviolet and green receptor classes.

inserts.title: Pigment absorption underlies receptor sensitivity
paragraphs: A visual pigment is a light-absorbing molecular complex containing an opsin protein, and the opsin contributes to the pigment's wavelength selectivity. A receptor's spectral sensitivity curve therefore follows the shape of the absorption of its pigment over much of the measured range.

DeVoe measured sensitivity on a logarithmic axis, on which equal steps represent multiplicative changes in light intensity. A decline of more than four logarithmic units beyond approximately 460 nm in the ultraviolet class therefore represents an enormous intensity difference, which marks strong spectral selectivity.

The green receptor class peaked near 532 nm in Phidippus, and the purified Rh1 pigment of Hasarius has an absorption maximum near 535 nm. Voltage sensitivity measured in cells and absorption measured in a purified pigment are complementary, and their similar green peaks support a pigment-based contribution to the green responses.
notes: Spectral sensitivity is measured physiologically in cells and absorption is measured biochemically in a pigment, so the two methods describe related properties of the same receptor channel.
What sensitivity compares.
The sensitivity measurement compares the light required to evoke a specified electrical response, which separates wavelength preference from the brightness the experimenter chose for each flash.
The ultraviolet class responds most effectively near 370 nanometers and loses sensitivity steeply toward longer wavelengths.
Reading a logarithmic axis.
A logarithmic axis represents multiplicative changes, so a large separation on the axis corresponds to a large difference in required intensity.
Pigment and cell measurements.
A purified pigment's absorption spectrum identifies a molecular property of the opsin complex.
The intact photoreceptor adds steps between photon absorption, membrane conductance and the recorded voltage.
Related species.
The close green peaks in Phidippus physiology and Hasarius pigment measurements are consistent with related spectral channels in the two species.

inserts.title: Wavelength changes blur across the retinal layers
paragraphs: Chromatic aberration is a wavelength-dependent difference in optical focus. Green and red light form their sharpest images at different positions, so the same object at the same distance produces a different pattern of focus across the receptor layers under different illumination.

In Hasarius adansoni, green-sensitive Rh1 occupies L1 and L2 and ultraviolet-sensitive Rh3 occupies L3 and L4. A green image is not sharply focused in L2 even though L2 contains green-sensitive receptors, so green-image blur is available to the retina.

Optical sharpness can therefore carry information independently of a pigment's wavelength preference. A green-sensitive receptor in a layer that is out of focus for green light receives a blurred image, and the amount of blur depends on object distance, which is the basis of the distance cue proposed in Hasarius.
notes: Chromatic aberration is an optical effect, not a claim about color perception, and it connects the pigment layers to a possible distance cue.
Focus depends on wavelength.
The wavelength of incident light changes the image plane relative to the receptor layers.
Red light has a longer focal length than green light in the measured optical system.
Where the green pigment sits.
Rh1 spans L1 and L2, and Rh3 occupies L3 and L4, according to antibody labeling and pigment expression measurements.
The result revises a simple assignment of one color to one depth.
Blur as information.
A green-sensitive receptor in L2 receives a blurred green image, and the degree of blur varies with the object's distance.
Optical sharpness can therefore carry distance information independently of the pigment's wavelength preference.
Layer assignment and function.
An antibody signal identifies where a protein is detected in the sectioned retina, and expression and purified absorption measurements add evidence about its identity and spectral properties.
Combining these with the optical measurements links spectral identity to retinal depth.

inserts.title: Controls separate optical focus from photon capture
paragraphs: Changing the wavelength of illumination changes two things at once: where the image is focused and how efficiently the light activates the visual pigment. A shortened jump under red light could therefore reflect defocus, reduced photon capture, or both.

Nagata and colleagues adjusted the green and red conditions to stimulate purified Rh1 with comparable efficiency, then raised the red intensity sixfold as an additional control. The jump-to-target-distance ratio remained approximately 0.89, close to the initial red value of approximately 0.90, so brighter red light did not restore the accuracy seen under green light.

Because the direction and approximate size of the error survived a sixfold increase in red intensity, a reduction in effective brightness is inadequate to explain the shortened jumps. The result supports a wavelength-dependent optical contribution to the distance estimate.
notes: A control isolates one explanation by removing the others, and the brightness manipulation separates the optical account from a photon-capture account.
Two explanations for the same error.
Red light shifts the focal plane and stimulates Rh1 less efficiently, so either factor could shorten the jump.
A dimmer effective stimulus could impair behavior even without a change in optical depth information.
The two controls.
Purified-pigment efficiency was used to match the effective stimulation of the green and red conditions.
Raising the red intensity sixfold left the ratio near 0.89, close to the 0.90 measured in the initial red condition.
Reading the ratio.
A ratio near one means the jump reached the target, and a ratio near 0.90 means an undershoot relative to the measured target distance.
Target distance was measured separately from jump distance, so the ratio compares the behavior with the real distance.
Scope of the control.
Purified-pigment efficiency constrains photon absorption by Rh1, whereas the voltage, adaptation and downstream gain of the intact receptor were not measured during these jumps.

inserts.title: A filter creates a spectral channel without a new opsin
paragraphs: A spectral filter changes which wavelengths reach a receptor by absorbing some more strongly than others. Habronattus pyrrithrix has a red, long-pass filter in part of its principal-eye retina, and a long-pass filter preferentially transmits longer wavelengths.

The filter acts before photon absorption by the pigment. Removing more short-wavelength light changes the effective sensitivity of an otherwise green-sensitive receptor, so combining the green pigment's sensitivity with the measured filter transmission predicts a peak near 626 nm.

An additional effective spectral channel can therefore arise by filtering an existing pigment class instead of adding a third opsin. With ultraviolet-sensitive pigment, unfiltered green receptors and filtered receptors, the retina has the optical basis for three spectral channels.
notes: A filter in front of a pigment can change a receptor's effective spectral sensitivity without changing its opsin.
How the filter works.
It absorbs short wavelengths before they reach the pigment, so the receptor effectively responds to longer wavelengths.
What was measured and what was calculated.
The paper measured the pigment properties, with peaks near 377 and 530 nm, and the filter's spectral transmission.
The published red curve combines those measurements and peaks near 626 nanometers.
Three channels from two pigments.
Trichromatic potential does not require three different opsin proteins here.
Ultraviolet, unfiltered green and filtered red channels are separable because the filter removes much of the light that the green pigment would otherwise absorb.
The cost of filtering.
The same absorption that shifts sensitivity leaves fewer photons for the filtered receptors, a potential cost under dim illumination.
Scope of the prediction.
The predicted red curve is a calculation from measured optical properties in Habronattus pyrrithrix.
The filter was found in other sampled Habronattus species but not in the sampled Salticus and Phidippus, which makes it a lineage-associated specialization.

inserts.title: Retinal movement has horizontal and torsional parts
paragraphs: Land's dissections in Metaphidippus identified six muscles on each principal eye. Four muscles displace the retinal assembly in horizontal or vertical directions, shifting the direction of gaze, and two thinner bands wrap around the tube and rotate it about its viewing axis.

Torsion is rotation around the optical axis, which changes the orientation of the receptor rows relative to a target without shifting where the eye points. Horizontal displacement changes the direction sampled, so the two actions change different properties of the image that the retina collects.

Because the large anterior lens stays fixed while the retina moves inside the eye, muscles acting on the tube can move the sampled image without a conspicuous rotation of the external eye. The mechanical arrangement supplies translation and rotation as separate actions.
notes: Six muscles give the principal retina two kinds of movement, a shift in the sampled direction and a rotation of the receptor array.
Four displacing muscles.
They move the retinal assembly horizontally or vertically behind the fixed lens.
The shift changes the direction of gaze.
Two wrapping bands.
They curve around the tube and rotate it about its viewing axis.
Rotating the retina changes the orientation of its receptor rows relative to a target.
Why the lens does not move.
The large anterior lens remains fixed, so the sampled image changes without a conspicuous rotation of the external eye.
What the dissections established.
Land established the muscle anatomy directly, which supports translation and rotation as possible actions.
Records of movement during behavior associate these actions with responses to targets.
Using the anatomy.
Because the retinal tube moves behind the fixed lens, the sampled direction and the orientation of the receptor rows can be changed independently.
Ophthalmoscopic records of retinal movement during target viewing relate these actions to responses.

inserts.title: Spontaneous shifts and evoked saccades are separable
paragraphs: A saccade is a rapid shift that repositions a visual sampling region. Land distinguished two classes of principal-eye movement: spontaneous activity, which occurs without an effective target, and saccades evoked by small target displacements.

Spontaneous activity included irregular shifts and periods of rapid movement, and it persisted when the visual field was blank and could occur after the eyes were covered. A visible target is therefore not required for these movements.

A small displacement of a target evoked an abrupt directed shift toward it followed by a slower return, a stereotyped sequence with a clear relation to the stimulus. Spontaneous records were more variable, and the two classes differ in how much they depend on visual input.
notes: Blank fields and covered eyes test whether a visible target is required for a movement, and they separate internally generated activity from visually evoked repositioning.
The tests for spontaneous activity.
Land compared the retinal activity under different visual conditions instead of assuming that every movement followed an external object.
Movements that continued with a blank field or with the eyes covered do not depend on a visible target.
The visually evoked class.
A target displacement produced an abrupt directed movement.
The slow return that followed differs from a sustained tracking response.
Why the distinction matters.
Persistence without ordinary visual input supports an internally generated component of eye movement.
A spontaneous shift and a target-evoked saccade are different response classes that appear in the same motor traces.
Timing of the evoked response.
The evoked shift is abrupt and directed toward the target, whereas the return to the starting position is slow.
Spontaneous movement continues during a blank field, so part of the movement is generated internally.

inserts.title: Open-loop tests remove feedback from the movement
paragraphs: An open-loop movement proceeds without the usual feedback about its ongoing effect. In a freely turning spider, the target shifts across the retina as the body rotates toward it, and that change can signal when to correct or stop the movement.

Land held the body of Metaphidippus fixed while its feet rotated a lightweight ring beneath it. The attempted turn was recorded, but it did not change the target's direction relative to the eyes, so the retinal consequence of the turn was removed.

Target movement and ring position were recorded separately with calibrated devices, which makes the attempted turn measurable without its visual consequences. Many turns still matched the initial target angle, so accurate turning can proceed without that feedback.
notes: Removing feedback allows the motor command itself to be measured, because the turn no longer changes what the eyes see.
Closed-loop turning.
In a free spider, rotation of the body changes the target's position on the retina.
That change can provide a signal for correcting or stopping the movement.
The ring preparation.
The body was held still while the feet moved the ring.
The attempted turn was recorded but did not create the normal change in target direction relative to the eyes.
Measuring the command.
Separate stimulus and ring traces make the distinction measurable.
The design removes the visual consequences of the body rotation.
Complete and partial turns.
Many responses were complete turns whose magnitude closely approximated the initial target angle, and other responses were smaller partial turns.
Why feedback matters for orienting.
Visual feedback is information about the consequences of an action returning through vision.
In a freely turning spider, it can reduce the remaining target error as the body rotates.

inserts.title: Masking tests dependence by removing one input
paragraphs: Masking an eye pair removes one source of visual input while leaving the rest of the animal intact, so a change in behavior after masking indicates that the covered input contributed to that behavior. Jakob and colleagues recorded internal principal-eye movements in restrained Phidippus audax before and after covering the anterior lateral eyes.

Moving disks with diameters of 3°, 4° and 5° and speeds from 2.77 to 15.13°/s were presented. Principal retinas followed the moving targets when the lateral eyes were available, and covering the lateral eyes disrupted the target-linked movements.

A control is needed to separate lost sensory guidance from damage to the motor apparatus. Principal-eye scanning of stationary cricket and oval stimuli persisted after masking, so the retina could still move and the deficit lay in guidance by the lateral eyes.
notes: A masking experiment tests whether one visual input is needed for a behavior, and a retained response serves as the control for general motor failure.
The logic of masking.
Covering one eye pair removes one source of visual information while the rest of the animal is unchanged.
A change in behavior therefore indicates that the covered input contributes.
Tracking with and without the lateral eyes.
Eye tracking recorded the position and orientation of the principal retinas in the restrained spider.
Several target sizes and speeds reduce dependence on one moving-dot condition.
The motor control.
A stationary target can be examined by moving the principal retina across it, without lateral-eye guidance of a moving target.
Retained scanning indicates that the mask did not abolish every principal-eye motor action, so scanning and tracking have different sensory dependencies.
Interpreting the result.
Masking provides stronger evidence about input dependence than observing coordination alone.
The measured output is internal retinal motion, which is distinct from whole-body orientation.

inserts.title: Spike sorting turns extracellular traces into units
paragraphs: An extracellular electrode detects the electrical activity of neurons near its tip, and each action potential appears as a brief waveform. When several neurons lie near the electrode, their spikes appear together in the same trace.

Spike sorting separates candidate units by waveform features, so the spike times of each unit can be analyzed on their own. Menda and colleagues paired visual stimulation with stable recordings lasting hours from Phidippus audax, using a glass-insulated tungsten electrode advanced through an opening of approximately 100–200 µm.

A spike raster records the times of action potentials across repeated presentations of the same stimulus. A unit that fires at consistent times in the sequence responds to that stimulus, and the stimulus position, velocity and direction are known independently of the recorded spikes.
notes: Extracellular recording measures spikes from outside the cells, and sorting provides candidate units whose responses can be compared across stimuli.
Why a small opening.
A spider's body pressure makes a large opening disruptive.
A small puncture reduces fluid loss and allows repeated stimulation during a stable recording.
From trace to units.
Extracellular spikes are detected outside the cells.
Waveform-based sorting distinguishes candidate units, although a sorted unit is not automatically a named anatomical neuron.
Rasters and repeated trials.
Repeated trajectories allow a response to be distinguished from unrelated fluctuations in firing.
The target sequence is controlled while the spike times are measured independently.
Where the recordings were made.
The electrode positions were in or near the arcuate body, which relates the physiology to central visual anatomy.
What a spike raster measures.
A raster plots action-potential times across repeated presentations, so the consistency of the timing can be assessed.
A restrained preparation allows recordings lasting hours while the visual display is controlled.

inserts.title: A receptive field combines position and time
paragraphs: A spatiotemporal receptive field describes how stimulation at different positions and at different times relates to a neuron's response. It therefore has a spatial arrangement and a time dependence, instead of a single preferred location.

Menda and colleagues presented rapidly changing checker patterns and related the pattern preceding each spike to the recorded spike times. For one unit, an organized receptive field emerged when both the principal and the lateral eyes were available, and it occupied an interval approximately 80–160 ms before the spikes.

Neither eye system alone recovered a structured field, so the unit is not explained by an independent response from either system. The dependence indicates nonlinear convergence of principal and secondary visual inputs at or before this unit.
inserts.citation: Menda et al. (2014); Steinhoff et al. (2020)
notes: A receptive field estimated with a checker stimulus has both a spatial arrangement and a time dependence, and eye masking tests which inputs create it.
The checker stimulus.
The stimulus varies many positions over time, and the pattern preceding each spike is related to the recorded spike times.
The resulting receptive field contains both a spatial arrangement and a time dependence.
The masking comparison.
Removing one eye system changed whether a structured field could be recovered.
A unit requiring both inputs is not adequately explained by a simple independent response from either one alone under the tested conditions.
The time window.
The 80–160 ms interval constrains the timing of the response-related pattern without counting synapses.
Internal-pattern controls reduced a display-related correlation.
Combining physiology with anatomy.
Combining this physiology in Phidippus with anatomy mapped in Marpissa supplies a comparative account of how principal and secondary inputs can converge.
Convergence.
Convergence is the arrival of multiple inputs at a processing region.
A unit that needs both eye systems to show a structured receptive field receives and combines input from the principal and secondary visual pathways.
